div.head: SUBSECT. 13.
Love of Gaming, &c., and pleasures immoderate; Causes.

l.hi: Alea Scylla vorax, species certissima furti,
Non contenta bonis animum quoque perfida mergit,

lg.l: Foeda, furax, infamis, iners, furiosa, ruina.
[Gaming’s a voracious Scylla, the surest kind of robbery,
Not content with goods, it treacherously engulfs the mind as well,
Loathsome, thieving, notorious, indolent, insane ruin.]

div.p:
For a little pleasure they take, and some small gains and gettings now and then, their wives and children are wringed in the meantime, & they themselves with loss of body and soul, rue it in the end. I will say nothing of those prodigious prodigals, perdendae pecuniae genitos [born to waste money], as he Sallust.taxed Antony, qui patrimonium sine ulla fori calumnia amittunt [who lose their money without any public disgrace], saith Tom. 3 Ser. de Alea.Cyprian, and Plutus in Aristop. calls all such gamesters madmen, Si in insanum hominem contigero [If I come to a crazy man …]. Spontaneum ad se trahunt furorem, & os & nares & oculos rivos faciunt furoris & diversoria [They voluntarily absorb madness, and make their mouths and nostrils and eyes into gutters and stews for frenzy], Chrys. hom. 71.mad Sybaritical spendthrifts, quique una comedunt patrimonia caena; that eat up all at a
breakfast, at a supper, or amongst Bawds, Parasites, and Players, consume themselves in an instant, as if they had flung it into Pascasius Justus lib. 1 de alea.Tiber, with great wagers, vain and idle expenses, &c., not themselves only, but even all their friends, as a man desperately swimming drowns him that comes to help him, by suretyship and borrowing they will willingly undo all their associates & allies. Seneca.Irati pecuniis, as he saith, angry with their money: Hall.What with a wanton eye, a liquorish tongue, and a gamesome hand, when they have undiscreetly impoverished themselves; mortgaged their wits together with their lands, and entombed their ancestors’ fair possessions in their bowels, they may lead the rest of their days in prison, as many times they do, there repent at leisure; and when all is gone begin to be thrifty: but sera est in fundo parsimonia, ’tis then too late to look about; their In Sat. 11. Sed deficiente crumena: & crescente gula quis te manet exitus ——— rebus in ventrem mersis [But with your money bag running out and your greed increasing, what fate awaits you? … Your stuff swallowed up in your belly].end is misery, sorrow, shame, and discontent. And well they deserve to be infamous and discontent, Spartian. Adriano.catomidiari in Amphitheatro [to be flogged in the amphitheatre], as by Hadrian the Emperor’s edict they were of old, decoctores bonorum suorum [spendthrifts of their goods], so he calls them, prodigal fools, to be publicly shamed, and hissed out of all societies, rather than to be pitied or relieved. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 6 cap. 10. Idem Gerbelius lib. 5 Grae. disc.The Tuscans and Boeotians brought their bankrupts into the marketplace in a bier with an empty purse carried before them, all the boys following, where they sat all day circumstante plebe [with the people standing round], to be infamous and ridiculous. At Fynes Morys.Padua in Italy they have a stone called the stone of Turpitude, near the Senate-house, where spendthrifts, and such as disclaim non-payment of debts, do sit with their hinder parts bare, that by that note of disgrace others may be terrified from all such vain expense, or borrowing more than they can tell how to pay. The Justinian. in Digestis.Civilians of old set guardians over such brainsick prodigals, as they did over madmen, to moderate their expenses, that they should not so loosely consume their fortunes, to the utter undoing of their Families.
I may not here omit those two main plagues, and common dotages of humankind, Wine and Women, which have infatuated and besotted Myriads of people: they go commonly together.

l.hi: Qui Vino indulget, quemque alea decoquit, ille

lg.l: [The man who gives himself up to wine, and bankrupts himself by gaming,

div.p: To whom is sorrow, saith Solomon, Prov. 23. 29, to whom is woe, but to such a one as loves drink? It causeth torture (vino tortus & ira), and bitterness of mind, Sirac. 31. 21. Vinum furoris, Jeremy calls it 25th cap., wine of madness, as well he may, for insanire facit sanos, it makes sound men sick and sad, and wise men Poculum quasi sinus, in quo saepe naufragium faciunt, jactura tum pecuniae tum mentis [The drinking-cup is like a gulf that brings about frequent shipwrecks, a throwing overboard not only of money but also of the mind], Erasm. in Proverb. calicum remiges, chil. 4 cent. 7 Prov. 41.mad, to say and do they know not what. Accidit hodie terribilis casus [A terrible misfortune happened today] (saith Ser. 33 ad frat. in Eremo.St. Austin), hear a miserable accident; Cyrillus’ son this day in his drink, matrem praegnantem nequiter oppressit, sororem violare voluit, patrem occidit fere, & duas alias sorores ad mortem vulneravit, would have violated his sister, killed his father, &c. A true saying it was of him, Vino dari laetitiam & dolorem, drink causeth mirth, and drink causeth sorrow, drink causeth poverty and want (Prov. 21), shame and disgrace. Multi ignobiles evasere ob vini potum, & (Austin) amissis honoribus profugi aberrarunt: many men have made a shipwreck of their fortunes, and go like rogues and beggars, having turned all their substance into aurum potabile, that otherwise might have lived in good worship and happy estate, and for a few hours’ pleasure, for their Hilary term’s but short, or free madness, as Seneca calls it, purchase unto themselves eternal tediousness and trouble.

That other madness is on women, Apostare facit cor: saith the wise man, Menander.atque homini cerebrum minuit [it makes the heart forsake its religion … and weakens a man’s brain]. Pleasant at first she is, like Dioscorides’ Rhododaphne, that fair plant to the eye, but poison to the taste, the rest as bitter as wormwood in the end (Prov. 5. 4) and sharp as a two-edged sword. And (7. 27) Her house is the way to hell, & goes down to the Chambers of death. What more sorrowful can be said? They are miserable in this life, mad, beasts, led like Prov. 7.Oxen to the slaughter: and that which is worse, whoremasters and drunkards shall be judged, amittunt gratiam, saith Austin, perdunt floriam, incurrunt damnationem aeternam. They lose grace and glory,

lg.l: Takes away the eternal glory of heaven …]

div.p: they gain Hell and eternal damnation.
